prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms and its development into an optical frequency standard at the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. After round 1 the case rests on the same tests that every leading group has applied to its own candidate: independent confirmation, a decisive and traceable contribution, and a credit that fits three names. B045 passes all three without arithmetic. Katori's magic-wavelength condition, which is a statement about differential polarisabilities and can be checked by calculation, lets thousands of atoms sit in a lattice without Doppler, recoil or trap-induced shifts. Ye's group then showed what that buys: uncertainties near 1e-18, a many-body-controlled lattice, and gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres. JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB and NIST build different clocks and compare them routinely, so this is not a single-laboratory claim. The chair asks what is new relative to 2005 and 2012. My answer is that the comb counts optical cycles and ion control isolates one quantum system, while the lattice clock solves the statistics problem that a single ion cannot, by interrogating a macroscopic ensemble without disturbing the transition. That is a new capability to ask nature a question about atomic structure and time, and it needs no redefinition of the second to justify it; I would keep the redefinition out of the citation. I also move my fallbacks. In round 1 I listed B008 as an alternative; I have dropped it, because the discussion has shown that the first ground-state demonstrations were near-simultaneous and any three of five names would be arbitrary. My preferred configuration itself has not changed. I was moved by Johansson and Kroll on B008, and by the chair's summary showing that B045 is named in seven of eight files, which I treat as evidence about acceptability only, not as a substitute for the physics.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against is distinctness: precision timekeeping has been rewarded in 1989, 2005 and 2012, and a sceptic can call the lattice clock a refinement of the same line. A second argument is that the redefinition of the second, geodesy and dark-matter searches are still prospective, so the largest consequences have not yet arrived. Third, the credit is not airtight: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto and colleagues in Katori's group, and Hall-type laser stabilisation sit outside two names, and Katori's priority for the magic-wavelength idea should be checked against the early Sr lattice work at other laboratories. I judge these real but not decisive. A citation worded on the lattice and magic-wavelength concept, not on 'better clocks' in general, answers the first; the other two are the ordinary price of a two-person prize in a field with many contributors.

responses.point: Johansson moved B045 to first place and calls it mature and robust, but says that his preference is partly a judgement on timing, that B026 is scientifically stronger and that the precision-timekeeping prizes of 1989, 2005 and 2012 make the novelty question serious.
responses.response: I accept your novelty point and have tried to answer it in the citation: the new element is many-atom interrogation without perturbing the transition, not a better number. I do not think your preference for B045 has to be only a judgement on timing, since the reproduction across laboratories is the kind of robustness you say you apply in your own field. On B026 I stay where I was in round 1: the 2025 overlap and the missing Girvin are real, and since you intend to recuse yourself from B026 the committee should not decide it through you. I also note that you said B008 left out Cleland and Painter. I agree, and I have withdrawn it as a fallback.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube with Halzen and Karle on the diffuse flux alone, states that source identification rests on one experiment so that waiting would make the prize premature, and names B045 as the safer, broader alternative.
responses.response: I take your statement that the diffuse flux is sufficient, and I defer to you and Mark Pearce on astrophysics; I have moved B016 into my alternatives for that reason. What keeps it behind B045 for me is the attribution that you yourself raise. Two names against AMANDA, other IceCube leaders and the analysis leads cannot be settled from the supplied text, and a collaboration prize needs the decisive contributors to be unambiguous. If you and the chair can show that Halzen and Karle are the right two on the record, and that the citation can be limited to the diffuse flux, I would count B016 as my next choice. You also describe B045 as the safer alternative; if the first-place camps cannot resolve attribution I will gladly be the consensus candidate for the committee, but only because the science and credit hold up.

responses.point: Kroll supports B045 with an identical pair, holds that the lattice clock differs from the comb and ion prizes because it addresses quantum-projection-noise and Doppler limits differently, and wants to check the Katori priority and the Takamoto and Lemonde contributions.
responses.response: We agree, and I want to sharpen the priority check. The magic-wavelength proposal was published by Katori and colleagues in 2003, and the first clock demonstration with Sr by Takamoto and Katori followed in 2005, but I am working from memory and cannot verify the dates against the supplied text. I would ask the committee to confirm that the concept and first demonstration are Katori's before we write them into the citation. I also repeat that your Hall-laboratory year is a mild link only; it does not touch Katori. For me it does not affect how I weigh your arguments, and I would ask that the committee record it, as you have done.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B040 from B038 and argues that the chain from the Kane-Mele theory to the HgTe transport measurement is traceable, that fifteen years of confirmation give a stable interpretation, and that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: Your reasoning that the interpretation has stopped moving is the same test I apply, and by that test B040 is mature; I do not dispute it. My difficulty is only the one you name. A three-name cap leaves out Hasan's 3D spectroscopy and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp where to look, and S.-C. Zhang is dead, so the trio is open to challenge whichever way it is drawn. The 2016 prize also rewarded topological phases, and the committee should be able to say in a sentence why this is distinct. I defer to you, Bernhard Mehlig and Eva Olsson on condensed matter. If the three of you can agree on one trio and a 2D-only citation that the committee finds fair, I would treat B040 as a serious contender and not only as a point of attribution.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, backs IceCube for the diffuse flux but says that the attribution is not as tidy as two names suggest, and that if the committee wants a consensus candidate then B045 is probably it.
responses.response: Thank you for being plain about your own taste bias, and for naming B045 as the probable consensus candidate. I do not want a prize chosen by counting second places, so I should say why I agree for scientific reasons: the credit is two names, the result is reproduced and compared across several national laboratories, and the physics is not going to be overturned. On the chair's question of whether the redefinition of the second must appear in the citation, my answer is no. I would keep it out of the citation, because the prospective consequence is not what is being rewarded, and mentioning it would invite the objection that we are awarding a metrology roadmap.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and whether my answer based on many-atom interrogation convinces others.

Whether Katori and Ye alone fairly capture the decisive contributions, given work at SYRTE (Lemonde), by Takamoto in Katori's group, and Hall-type laser stabilisation; the dates for Katori's magic-wavelength priority are recalled from memory.
Whether the attribution for B016 (Halzen, Karle) can be shown to be right, since I would then regard it as a serious fallback.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would make B045 stronger or only delay it.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I am a theoretical atomic physicist at Stockholm University and my known close collaboration is with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, none of whom are on the shortlist. My field is adjacent to B045 and B007 but I have no personal, collaborative or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names; I do not regard anything in my record as recusal-level for my preferred configuration or alternatives.
